---
title: "Is fastsae Better? Accuracy, Speed and Memory against sae, emdi and tipsae"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.6, dpi = 110
)
library(ggplot2)

ext_dir <- Filter(dir.exists, c(
  file.path("..", "..", "inst", "extdata"),
  file.path("inst", "extdata")
))[1]
rd <- function(f) {
  p <- file.path(ext_dir, f)
  if (length(p) == 1 && file.exists(p)) readRDS(p) else NULL
}
sfh <- rd("eval_sfh_accuracy.rds")
bta <- rd("eval_beta_accuracy.rds")
res <- rd("eval_resources.rds")
have <- !is.null(sfh) && !is.null(bta) && !is.null(res)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = have)

method_labels <- c(
  fastsae = "fastsae::eblup_sfh", sae = "sae::mseSFH", emdi = "emdi::fh",
  inla = "fastsae, INLA", jax = "fastsae, NumPyro (CPU)", metal = "fastsae, NumPyro (Apple GPU)",
  tipsae = "tipsae (Stan)"
)
method_colours <- c(
  fastsae = "#1D6A5C", sae = "#C0392B", emdi = "#7B5EA7",
  inla = "#1D6A5C", jax = "#E69F00", metal = "#7B5EA7", tipsae = "#C0392B"
)
sfh_scen_labels <- c(
  base = "Base (grid, D = 100, rho = 0.5)", rho_low = "rho = 0.2", rho_high = "rho = 0.8",
  rho_edge = "rho = 0.95", psi_low = "psi / sigma2 = 0.5", psi_high = "psi / sigma2 = 2",
  D50 = "D = 50", D500 = "D = 500", mys = "Real map (mys_proxmat, D = 42)"
)
beta_scen_labels <- c(
  base = "Base (grid, D = 50)", spat_low = "sigma_s = 0.2", spat_high = "sigma_s = 1",
  kappa_low = "kappa = 10", kappa_high = "kappa = 100", voronoi = "Irregular map (D = 50)"
)
f2 <- function(x, d = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
fmt_s <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "-", ifelse(x < 10, sprintf("%.2f s", x), sprintf("%s s", format(round(x), big.mark = ","))))
fmt_mb <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "-", ifelse(x >= 1024, sprintf("%.2f GB", x / 1024), sprintf("%.0f MB", x)))
# mean and Monte Carlo standard error over independent replicates
mc <- function(x) c(mean = mean(x), mcse = stats::sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)))
```

```{r missing, eval = !have, results = "asis"}
cat("> The result files (`inst/extdata/eval_*.rds`) are not available, so this article shows no results.",
    "Run `sh benchmarks/eval/run_overnight.sh` from the package root to create them.\n")
```

This article asks whether **fastsae** is better than the packages it is usually compared with, for
two models and in three respects: accuracy of the estimates, speed and memory. The answer is
given separately for each respect. Where fastsae is not better, the article says so.

- **A. Spatial Fay-Herriot model (SAR random effects, frequentist).** `fastsae::eblup_sfh()`
  against `sae::mseSFH()` (Molina and Marhuenda, 2015) and `emdi::fh(correlation = "spatial")`
  (Kreutzmann et al., 2019).
- **B. Spatial Beta model (Bayesian).** `fastsae::hb_area(family = "beta")` with INLA
  (`inla_engine()`, an approximation; Rue et al., 2009) and with MCMC in NumPyro
  (`jax_engine()`), against `tipsae::fit_sae()` (MCMC in Stan; De Nicolò and Gardini, 2024).

## Summary

```{r summary-numbers}
# SFH
sfh_fail <- aggregate(failed ~ method, sfh$fits, sum)
sfh_n <- aggregate(failed ~ method, sfh$fits, length)
sfh_reps <- sfh$reps
sfh_wide <- reshape(aggregate(mse ~ scenario + method, sfh_reps, mean), idvar = "scenario",
                    timevar = "method", direction = "wide")
sfh_max_rmse_diff <- max(abs(sqrt(sfh_wide$mse.fastsae) - sqrt(sfh_wide$mse.sae)),
                         abs(sqrt(sfh_wide$mse.fastsae) - sqrt(sfh_wide$mse.emdi)))
rc <- res$cells
t_of <- function(model, method, D, col = "time_warm") {
  v <- rc[rc$model == model & rc$method == method & rc$D == D, col]
  if (length(v)) v[1] else NA_real_
}
m_of <- function(model, method, D) t_of(model, method, D, "peak_increase_mb")
sfh_Dmax <- max(rc$D[rc$model == "sfh"])
beta_Dmax <- max(rc$D[rc$model == "beta"])
beta_Dmin <- min(rc$D[rc$model == "beta"])
# Beta
br <- bta$reps
beta_acc <- aggregate(cbind(mse, cover) ~ scenario + method, br, mean)
beta_acc$rmse <- sqrt(beta_acc$mse)
```

| Respect | Spatial Fay-Herriot | Spatial Beta |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Accuracy** | **The same.** The three packages fit the same model by the same REML criterion and give the same estimates, except in a few data sets near the boundary of $\rho$; on the data sets where all fitted, their RMSEs differ by at most `r sprintf("%.0e", sfh_max_rmse_diff)`. fastsae fitted every data set (`r sfh_fail$failed[sfh_fail$method == "fastsae"]` failures out of `r sfh_n$failed[sfh_n$method == "fastsae"]`); `sae` and `emdi` stopped with an error `r sfh_fail$failed[sfh_fail$method == "sae"]` and `r sfh_fail$failed[sfh_fail$method == "emdi"]` times. | **About the same, not uniformly better.** INLA and NumPyro agree closely; tipsae is as accurate in most scenarios, less accurate with a strong spatial effect (where its chains often did not converge) and slightly more accurate with a low Beta precision. All three under-cover in the hardest scenarios. |
| **Speed** | **Faster.** At $D = `r format(sfh_Dmax, big.mark = ",")`$: `r fmt_s(t_of("sfh", "fastsae", sfh_Dmax))` against `r fmt_s(t_of("sfh", "sae", sfh_Dmax))` (`sae`) and `r fmt_s(t_of("sfh", "emdi", sfh_Dmax))` (`emdi`). | **INLA is much faster** (`r fmt_s(t_of("beta", "inla", beta_Dmax))` at $D = `r format(beta_Dmax, big.mark = ",")`$ against `r fmt_s(t_of("beta", "tipsae", beta_Dmax))` for tipsae). NumPyro on the CPU is 2 to 5 times faster than tipsae per fit, and up to 3 times per effective draw. NumPyro on the Apple GPU was the slowest at every size measured. |
| **Memory** | **Lower or about the same, by a much smaller margin than the time.** At $D = `r format(sfh_Dmax, big.mark = ",")`$: `r fmt_mb(m_of("sfh", "fastsae", sfh_Dmax))` against `r fmt_mb(m_of("sfh", "sae", sfh_Dmax))` and `r fmt_mb(m_of("sfh", "emdi", sfh_Dmax))`. | **Mixed.** At $D = `r beta_Dmin`$ tipsae used the least memory (`r fmt_mb(m_of("beta", "tipsae", beta_Dmin))`, INLA `r fmt_mb(m_of("beta", "inla", beta_Dmin))`); at $D = `r format(beta_Dmax, big.mark = ",")`$ INLA used the least (`r fmt_mb(m_of("beta", "inla", beta_Dmax))` against `r fmt_mb(m_of("beta", "tipsae", beta_Dmax))`). NumPyro needs 700-900 MB at every size, mostly for Python and JAX. |

All results come from one machine (`r res$meta$cpu`, `r res$meta$cores` cores,
`r round(res$meta$ram_gb)` GB RAM, no NVIDIA GPU); see [Machine and versions](#machine-and-versions).

---

## Design of the study

The study follows the ADEMP structure of Morris, White and Crowther (2019): aims,
data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods and performance measures.

**Aims.** To compare, on data with known truth, the accuracy of the area estimates and of the
model parameters, and to measure the time and memory of one fit.

### Data-generating mechanisms

Both studies are model-based: the covariates and the sampling variances are fixed within a
scenario, and the random effects and the sampling errors are drawn anew in each replicate.
Each scenario changes one factor of a base scenario. The parameter values were chosen for this
study; the model forms follow the literature cited.

**A. Spatial Fay-Herriot** (SAR random effects; Petrucci and Salvati, 2006; Pratesi and
Salvati, 2008):

$$y_d = x_d^\top\beta + u_d + e_d,\quad u = (I - \rho W)^{-1}\varepsilon,\quad
\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I),\quad e_d \sim N(0, \psi_d),$$

with $\beta = (1, 0.8, -0.5)$, $x_{1d} \sim N(0, 1)$, $x_{2d} \sim U(0, 1)$, $\sigma^2 = 1$,
$\psi_d = r\,\sigma^2 u_d$, $u_d \sim U(0.5, 1.5)$, and $W$ the row-standardised queen
contiguity matrix of a regular grid, or of the 42 districts of the `mys_proxmat` data. Base
scenario: $D = 100$, $\rho = 0.5$, $r = 1$. Others: $\rho \in \{0.2, 0.8, 0.95\}$,
$r \in \{0.5, 2\}$, $D \in \{50, 500\}$ and the real map. **`r sfh$meta$R_reps` replicates**
per scenario.

**B. Spatial Beta** (Beta regression for proportions, Ferrari and Cribari-Neto, 2004; Beta
area-level model, Janicki, 2020; random effect of Besag, York and Mollié, 1991, scaled as in
Riebler et al., 2016):

$$y_d \sim \mathrm{Beta}\big(\mu_d\kappa_d,\,(1 - \mu_d)\kappa_d\big),\quad
\mathrm{logit}(\mu_d) = x_d^\top\beta + v_d + s_d,\quad v_d \sim N(0, \sigma_v^2),\quad
s = \sigma_s\,\tilde s,$$

where $\tilde s$ is an intrinsic CAR (ICAR) field on the queen adjacency graph, scaled to a
geometric mean marginal variance of 1. $\beta = (-1, 0.5, -0.4)$, $x_{1d} \sim N(0, 1)$,
$x_{2d} \sim U(-1, 1)$, $\sigma_v = 0.2$, $\kappa_d = \kappa\,e^{a_d}$ with $a_d \sim U(-0.5, 0.5)$.
The sampling variance is estimated from the direct estimate, $\hat V_d = y_d(1 - y_d)/(\kappa_d + 1)$,
as a survey would. Base scenario: a $5 \times 10$ grid ($D = 50$), $\sigma_s = 0.5$,
$\kappa = 25$. Others: $\sigma_s \in \{0.2, 1\}$, $\kappa \in \{10, 100\}$ and an irregular map
(Voronoi tessellation of 50 random points). The real map of `mys_proxmat` is not used here:
tipsae needs polygons, and `mys_proxmat` is only a matrix. **`r bta$meta$R_reps` replicates** per
scenario.

**Why $D = 50$ and 100 replicates for the Beta model.** The MCMC fits take about a minute each
(tipsae) under parallel load, so a larger $D$ or more replicates would not fit in one overnight
run; the speed and memory measurements go up to $D = `r format(beta_Dmax, big.mark = ",")`$.
With 100 replicates of 50 areas, the Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) of a coverage rate is
shown next to every estimate.

### Estimands and methods

The estimands are the area quantities ($\theta_d = x_d^\top\beta + u_d$ for the SFH model,
$\mu_d$ for the Beta model) and the model parameters.

**Spatial Fay-Herriot.** All three packages use REML and the analytical MSE of
Prasad-Rao type. In a pilot on one data set, the three gave the same coefficients, variance,
$\rho$, EBLUPs and MSEs up to about $10^{-15}$. The documented differences of fastsae (an
estimate $|\hat\rho| \ge 0.999$ is treated as fixed in the MSE; see `?eblup_sfh` and `NEWS.md`)
apply only on the boundary. The 95% intervals are $\hat\theta_d \pm 1.96\sqrt{\mathrm{mse}_d}$.

**Spatial Beta.** tipsae's `spatial_error = TRUE` adds an unstructured and a scaled ICAR effect
(read from its Stan code: `reffs = v + s` with `s = sigma_s * s_raw / scales_ICAR`). The same
structure in fastsae is `spatial = "bym"` (iid + scaled Besag), which is used here, with the
defaults of each package otherwise. The differences that remain cannot be removed through the
user interfaces:

| | fastsae (INLA and NumPyro) | tipsae |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Inference | INLA: Laplace approximation. NumPyro: NUTS, 2 chains of 1,000 draws after 500 warm-up | NUTS in Stan, 4 chains of 1,000 draws after 1,000 warm-up |
| SD of the area effects | half-normal(1) on each SD | half-normal(2.5) on each SD |
| Coefficients | $N(0, 1000)$, intercept flat (INLA) or nearly flat (NumPyro) | $N(0, 2.5^2)$ on standardised covariates (tipsae scales them; its coefficients are converted back for this article) |
| Beta precision | fixed per area at $\hat\mu_d(1 - \hat\mu_d)/\hat V_d - 1$, with $\hat\mu_d$ from a first fit (the model is fitted twice) | inside the model: $\phi_d = (\mu_d(1 - \mu_d) - \hat V_d)/\hat V_d$ |

So the comparison is between what a user gets from each package with its defaults, not between
two approximations of one posterior.

### Performance measures

- Per replicate, averaged over the areas: bias, mean squared error, coverage of the 95%
  intervals and their width. The tables report the mean over replicates, with its MCSE
  (standard deviation over replicates divided by $\sqrt{R}$), and RMSE as the square root of the
  mean squared error.
- Per area, over replicates: the relative RMSE $\mathrm{RMSE}_d / \bar\theta_d$ (Beta model only,
  where the truth is positive).
- Model parameters: estimates against the true values; for the SFH model, the share of estimates
  of $\rho$ on the boundary.
- MCMC: the largest R-hat and the smallest effective sample size over the reported parameters,
  and divergent transitions (Vehtari et al., 2021). A fit with R-hat > 1.05, an ESS below 100 per
  chain, or a divergence is counted as not converged; **it is kept in all accuracy measures**.
- Failed fits are counted. Accuracy is compared on the replicates where every method returned a
  fit, so that all methods see the same data sets.
- Time and memory are measured separately, one fit per R process on an idle machine (see
  [Speed](#speed) and [Memory](#memory)).

### Simulation procedure

For each scenario $k$:

1. **Fix the design** (seed $1000 + k$): the map and its adjacency matrix, the covariates
   $x_{1d}, x_{2d}$, and the sampling variances $\psi_d$ (SFH) or the Beta precisions $\kappa_d$.
   These stay the same in all replicates of the scenario.
2. **For each replicate** $r = 1, \dots, R$ (seed $10^5 k + r$):
   a. Draw the random effects ($u$ for the SFH model; $v$ and $s$ for the Beta model) and compute
      the true area quantities $\theta_{dr}$ ($x_d^\top\beta + u_d$, or $\mu_d$).
   b. Draw the direct estimates: $y_d = \theta_{dr} + e_d$ with $e_d \sim N(0, \psi_d)$, or
      $y_d \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\mu_d\kappa_d, (1 - \mu_d)\kappa_d)$ with the sampling variance
      $\hat V_d = y_d(1 - y_d)/(\kappa_d + 1)$ computed from $y_d$.
   c. Fit every method to this same data set. The SFH packages get the row-standardised $W$; for
      the Beta model fastsae gets the binary adjacency matrix and tipsae the polygons of the same
      map. The MCMC methods use seed $r$.
   d. Keep, per area, the estimate $\hat\theta_{dr}$ and its 95% interval, and, per fit, the model
      parameters, the convergence diagnostics, the warnings and the time. A fit that stops with an
      error is kept as a failure with its error message.
3. **Summarise** on the replicates where every method returned a fit:
   $\mathrm{Bias}_d = R^{-1}\sum_r(\hat\theta_{dr} - \theta_{dr})$,
   $\mathrm{RMSE}_d = \{R^{-1}\sum_r(\hat\theta_{dr} - \theta_{dr})^2\}^{1/2}$, and the share of
   replicates whose interval contains $\theta_{dr}$, plus the per-replicate averages over the
   areas described above.

**Intervals.** For the SFH model, $\hat\theta_d \pm 1.96\sqrt{\mathrm{mse}_d}$ with the analytical
MSE of each package. For the Beta model, the equal-tailed 95% posterior interval of $\mu_d$ (the
2.5% and 97.5% posterior quantiles): from INLA's posterior marginals, from the NumPyro draws, and
from the Stan summary of tipsae.

**What varies between replicates.** The true values change from one replicate to the next, since
the random effects are redrawn: bias, RMSE and coverage are averages over realisations of the
model, for a fixed design. This is a model-based simulation; the
[finite population article](finite-population-validation.html) shows a design-based one, in which
a fixed population is sampled repeatedly.

**How it was run.** The replicates were split into tasks of one scenario, one method and a block
of 100 (SFH) or 25 (Beta) replicates, and six tasks ran at a time. Every replicate was saved to its
own file, so an interrupted run resumes where it stopped. The times recorded in this stage were
measured under that parallel load and are not used in [Speed](#speed).

---

## A. Spatial Fay-Herriot

### Accuracy of the area estimates

```{r sfh-accuracy}
a_ <- sfh_reps[sfh_reps$method == "fastsae", ]; b_ <- sfh_reps[sfh_reps$method == "sae", ]
a_ <- a_[order(a_$scenario, a_$rep), ]; b_ <- b_[order(b_$scenario, b_$rep), ]
fit_f <- sfh$fits[sfh$fits$method == "fastsae", ]; fit_s <- sfh$fits[sfh$fits$method == "sae", ]
k_ <- a_[abs(a_$cover - b_$cover) > 1e-12, c("scenario", "rep")]
k_ <- merge(merge(k_, fit_f[, c("scenario", "rep", "rho")]),
            setNames(fit_s[, c("scenario", "rep", "rho")], c("scenario", "rep", "rho_sae")))
n_common <- nrow(a_)
n_cov_diff <- nrow(k_)
n_cov_same <- sum(abs(k_$rho - k_$rho_sae) < 1e-6)
fl_ <- merge(sfh$fits[sfh$fits$method == "sae" & sfh$fits$failed, c("scenario", "rep")],
             fit_f[, c("scenario", "rep", "rho", "sigma2")])
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sfh_scen_labels), function(s) {
  r <- sfh_reps[sfh_reps$scenario == s, ]
  row <- function(m) {
    x <- r[r$method == m, ]
    c(rmse = sqrt(mean(x$mse)), rmse_se = stats::sd(x$mse) / sqrt(nrow(x)) / (2 * sqrt(mean(x$mse))),
      cover = mean(x$cover), cover_se = stats::sd(x$cover) / sqrt(nrow(x)), width = mean(x$width))
  }
  f <- row("fastsae"); a <- row("sae"); e <- row("emdi")
  fl <- sfh$fits[sfh$fits$scenario == s, ]
  data.frame(
    Scenario = sfh_scen_labels[[s]],
    `Replicates (common)` = nrow(r[r$method == "fastsae", ]),
    `RMSE (MCSE)` = sprintf("%s (%s)", f2(f[["rmse"]]), f2(f[["rmse_se"]])),
    `Coverage (MCSE)` = sprintf("%s (%s)", pct(f[["cover"]]), pct(f[["cover_se"]])),
    `Width` = f2(f[["width"]]),
    `Max. RMSE diff. sae / emdi` = sprintf("%.1e / %.1e", abs(f[["rmse"]] - a[["rmse"]]), abs(f[["rmse"]] - e[["rmse"]])),
    `Coverage sae / emdi` = sprintf("%s / %s", pct(a[["cover"]]), pct(e[["cover"]])),
    `Failed fits fastsae / sae / emdi` = sprintf("%d / %d / %d", sum(fl$failed[fl$method == "fastsae"]),
                                                  sum(fl$failed[fl$method == "sae"]), sum(fl$failed[fl$method == "emdi"])),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrr")
```

The RMSE, coverage and width are those of fastsae; the other two columns show how far `sae` and
`emdi` are from them on the same data sets. Every package keeps close to the nominal 95% in every
scenario, and the estimates are the same in all but a few data sets:

- Away from the boundary of $\rho$, the EBLUPs and MSEs of fastsae and `sae` differed by at most
  about $2 \times 10^{-4}$, the size of the convergence tolerance of the two algorithms.
- In `r n_cov_diff` of the `r n_common` common data sets, the coverage differed. In
  `r n_cov_same` of them both packages gave the same estimate $\hat\rho = -1$; fastsae then treats
  $\rho$ as fixed in the MSE (a documented difference, see `?eblup_sfh`), which gives narrower
  intervals. In the other `r n_cov_diff - n_cov_same`, the two packages ended at different
  estimates of $\rho$ (for example $-1$ in `sae` and $0.999$ in fastsae): the restricted likelihood
  has more than one local maximum near the boundary, and fastsae maximises it under the
  constraints $\sigma^2 \ge 0$, $|\rho| \le 0.999$. Which of the two maxima is higher was not
  checked.

**Failed fits.**

```{r sfh-errors}
fe <- sfh$fits[sfh$fits$failed, ]
fe$Error <- ifelse(grepl("comparison \\(>=\\)", fe$error), "diff >= PRECISION: comparison is possible only for atomic and list types",
             ifelse(grepl("singular", fe$error), "singular system (solve() or LAPACK dgesv)", fe$error))
knitr::kable(as.data.frame.matrix(table(fe$Error, factor(fe$method, levels = c("fastsae", "sae", "emdi")))),
             align = "rrr")
```

Most failures came from solving a singular system. The others are an error in the convergence
check of the Fisher-scoring loop of `sae::eblupSFH()` (`diff >= PRECISION`), raised by `sae`
itself, not by the code of this study. The failures are concentrated in the scenarios that push $\hat\rho$ or $\hat\sigma^2$ towards a boundary:
large sampling variances, a strong correlation, few areas, and the real map. fastsae maximises the restricted likelihood
under the constraints $\sigma^2 \ge 0$, $|\rho| \le 0.999$ and returned an estimate every time.

### Model parameters

```{r sfh-params}
f <- sfh$fits[!sfh$fits$failed, ]
f$rho_true <- vapply(f$scenario, function(s) sfh$scenarios[[s]]$rho, 0)
pt <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sfh_scen_labels), function(s) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("fastsae", "sae"), function(m) {
    x <- f[f$scenario == s & f$method == m, ]
    data.frame(
      Scenario = sfh_scen_labels[[s]], Package = m,
      `True rho` = f2(x$rho_true[1], 2),
      `Mean rho-hat (MCSE)` = sprintf("%s (%s)", f2(mean(x$rho)), f2(stats::sd(x$rho) / sqrt(nrow(x)))),
      `Mean sigma2-hat (true 1)` = f2(mean(x$sigma2)),
      `rho-hat on boundary` = pct(mean(abs(x$rho) >= 0.999)),
      `Mean beta1-hat (true 0.8)` = f2(mean(x$beta1)),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }))
}))
knitr::kable(pt, row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrrr")
```

`emdi` gave the same parameters as `sae` and is left out of the table. REML underestimates
$\rho$, most strongly with few areas or large sampling variances, and the bias shrinks as $D$
grows: this is a property of the estimator, shared by all three packages, not of an
implementation. The averages of `sae` leave out its failed fits. In the `r nrow(fl_)` data sets
where `sae` failed, fastsae's $\hat\rho$ was on the boundary in `r sum(abs(fl_$rho) >= 0.999)`,
and $\hat\sigma^2$ was often small (median `r f2(stats::median(fl_$sigma2), 2)` against a true 1).

## B. Spatial Beta

### Accuracy of the area estimates

```{r beta-accuracy}
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(beta_scen_labels), function(s) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("inla", "jax", "tipsae"), function(m) {
    x <- br[br$scenario == s & br$method == m, ]
    a <- bta$area[bta$area$scenario == s & bta$area$method == m, ]
    rm <- sqrt(mean(x$mse))
    data.frame(
      Scenario = beta_scen_labels[[s]], Method = method_labels[[m]],
      `RMSE (MCSE)` = sprintf("%s (%s)", f2(rm, 4), f2(stats::sd(x$mse) / sqrt(nrow(x)) / (2 * rm), 4)),
      `Mean relative RMSE` = pct(mean(a$rmse / a$truth)),
      `Mean abs. bias` = f2(mean(abs(a$bias)), 4),
      `Coverage (MCSE)` = sprintf("%s (%s)", pct(mean(x$cover)), pct(stats::sd(x$cover) / sqrt(nrow(x)))),
      `Width` = f2(mean(x$width)),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }))
}))
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrrr")
```

```{r beta-coverage, fig.height = 4.2}
cv <- aggregate(cover ~ scenario + method, br, function(v) c(m = mean(v), se = stats::sd(v) / sqrt(length(v))))
cv <- data.frame(scenario = cv$scenario, method = cv$method, m = cv$cover[, "m"], se = cv$cover[, "se"])
cv$scenario_f <- factor(beta_scen_labels[cv$scenario], levels = rev(beta_scen_labels))
cv$method_f <- factor(method_labels[cv$method], levels = method_labels[c("inla", "jax", "tipsae")])
ggplot(cv, aes(m, scenario_f, colour = method_f)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = m - 1.96 * se, xmax = m + 1.96 * se), position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(method_colours[c("inla", "jax", "tipsae")], method_labels[c("inla", "jax", "tipsae")])) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(100 * x, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Coverage of the 95% intervals (with 95% Monte Carlo interval)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

- **INLA and NumPyro** give nearly the same accuracy in every scenario: the approximation of INLA
  costs nothing measurable here.
- **tipsae** is as accurate as fastsae in most scenarios. With a strong spatial effect
  ($\sigma_s = 1$) its RMSE is clearly larger; this is also the scenario where its chains most
  often did not converge (next section). With a low Beta precision ($\kappa = 10$) its RMSE is
  slightly smaller than that of fastsae, possibly because it models the precision inside the model
  instead of fixing it from a first fit; this study cannot separate that from the prior.
- tipsae's intervals covered the truth less often than those of fastsae with INLA in every
  scenario, by 0.1 to 1.7 percentage points (the Monte Carlo intervals overlap in some).
- tipsae has the largest mean absolute bias of the area estimates in every scenario, although
  the bias is small next to the RMSE for all methods.
- **All methods under-cover** when the precision is low or the spatial effect strong, by a
  similar amount: with $D = 50$, the hyperparameters are poorly determined by the data.

### Model parameters

```{r beta-params}
f <- bta$fits[!bta$fits$failed, ]
pt <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(beta_scen_labels), function(s) {
  sc <- bta$scenarios[[s]]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("inla", "jax", "tipsae"), function(m) {
    x <- f[f$scenario == s & f$method == m, ]
    data.frame(
      Scenario = beta_scen_labels[[s]], Method = method_labels[[m]],
      `beta1 (0.5)` = f2(stats::median(x$beta1)), `beta2 (-0.4)` = f2(stats::median(x$beta2)),
      `sigma_v (true)` = sprintf("%s (%s)", f2(stats::median(x$sigma_v)), sc$sigma_v),
      `sigma_s (true)` = sprintf("%s (%s)", f2(stats::median(x$sigma_s)), sc$sigma_s),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }))
}))
knitr::kable(pt, row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrr")
```

Medians over the replicates of the posterior medians. The three methods recover the coefficients
equally well. The unstructured SD $\sigma_v$ is overestimated by all three, more when the precision
is low: with 50 areas, it is hard to tell from the spatial effect and from the sampling noise, and
its posterior is pulled towards the prior.

### Convergence of the MCMC fits

```{r beta-convergence}
g <- f[f$method != "inla", ]
g$chains <- ifelse(g$method == "jax", 2, 4)
cvg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(beta_scen_labels), function(s) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("jax", "tipsae"), function(m) {
    x <- g[g$scenario == s & g$method == m, ]
    bad <- x$rhat_max > 1.05 | x$ess_min < 100 * x$chains | x$divergences > 0
    data.frame(
      Scenario = beta_scen_labels[[s]], Method = method_labels[[m]], Fits = nrow(x),
      `R-hat > 1.05` = sum(x$rhat_max > 1.05),
      `ESS < 100 per chain` = sum(x$ess_min < 100 * x$chains),
      `Any divergence` = sum(x$divergences > 0),
      `Not converged (any)` = sum(bad),
      `Median smallest ESS` = round(stats::median(x$ess_min)),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }))
}))
knitr::kable(cvg, row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrrrr")
```

With their default settings, **neither MCMC method converged reliably** by these criteria: in every
scenario between a quarter and nearly all of the fits had a too small ESS for some parameter, both had divergent transitions in many fits (NumPyro most often with $\kappa = 100$ and
$\sigma_s = 1$, tipsae with $\kappa = 10$ and $\sigma_s = 1$), and tipsae had an R-hat above
1.05 in a third of the fits with a strong spatial effect. NumPyro's default of 2 chains of 1,000
draws gives fewer draws than tipsae's 4 chains of 1,000, so its ESS is lower for that reason
alone.
The defaults of both are meant for a first look; for reported results, longer chains (for
NumPyro, `jax_engine(warmup = , samples = )`) and a check of the diagnostics are needed. INLA has
no such diagnostics; its accuracy above is the check.

The two smallest ESS values are not computed in the same way: for NumPyro it is the smallest
rank-normalised bulk or tail ESS over the hyperparameters, coefficients and area means (as
reported by fastsae); for tipsae it is the smallest `n_eff` of `rstan` over all parameters of the
Stan summary. They are comparable in size, not exactly.

---

## Speed

Each cell below is one R process that fits the same data set several times (two for the slowest
cells, three otherwise); the first fit includes start-up costs (compilation of the JAX model,
the first call of Stan), and the table shows the median of the later ones. The processes ran one
after another on an otherwise idle machine. The SFH data are the base scenario on a grid of $D$
cells; the Beta data are the base scenario of the accuracy study.

```{r speed-table}
sp <- rc[rc$method != "baseline", ]
mk <- function(model, methods) {
  x <- sp[sp$model == model & sp$method %in% methods, ]
  w <- reshape(x[, c("method", "D", "time_warm")], idvar = "D", timevar = "method", direction = "wide")
  w <- w[order(w$D), ]
  out <- data.frame(D = format(w$D, big.mark = ","))
  for (m in methods) out[[method_labels[[m]]]] <- fmt_s(w[[paste0("time_warm.", m)]])
  out
}
knitr::kable(mk("sfh", c("fastsae", "sae", "emdi")), row.names = FALSE, align = "rrrr",
             caption = "Spatial Fay-Herriot: REML fit and analytical MSE (warm time)")
knitr::kable(mk("beta", c("inla", "jax", "metal", "tipsae")), row.names = FALSE, align = "rrrrr",
             caption = "Spatial Beta (warm time)")
```

```{r speed-plot, fig.width = 4.6, fig.height = 4.2, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "49%"}
speed_plot <- function(model, methods, title) {
  x <- sp[sp$model == model & sp$method %in% methods, ]
  x$method_f <- factor(method_labels[x$method], levels = method_labels[methods])
  ggplot(x, aes(D, time_warm, colour = method_f)) +
    geom_line() + geom_point() +
    scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(method_colours[methods], method_labels[methods])) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Number of areas D (log scale)", y = "Seconds per fit (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
}
speed_plot("sfh", c("fastsae", "sae", "emdi"), "A. Spatial Fay-Herriot")
speed_plot("beta", c("inla", "jax", "metal", "tipsae"), "B. Spatial Beta")
```

For the MCMC methods, the time per fit depends on the number of draws, so the time per effective
draw (warm time divided by the smallest ESS of that fit) is the fairer comparison:

```{r time-per-ess}
x <- sp[sp$model == "beta" & sp$method %in% c("jax", "metal", "tipsae"), ]
w <- reshape(transform(x, tpe = time_warm / ess_min)[, c("method", "D", "tpe")], idvar = "D",
             timevar = "method", direction = "wide")
w <- w[order(w$D), ]
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  D = format(w$D, big.mark = ","),
  `NumPyro (CPU)` = sprintf("%.3f s", w$tpe.jax),
  `NumPyro (Apple GPU)` = sprintf("%.3f s", w$tpe.metal),
  tipsae = sprintf("%.3f s", w$tpe.tipsae),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "rrrr")
```

- **Spatial Fay-Herriot:** fastsae is faster at every size, and the gap grows with $D$ (sparse
  Cholesky factorisations instead of dense $D \times D$ inverses). With a few dozen areas all
  three take a fraction of a second, and the difference does not matter in practice.
- **Spatial Beta:** INLA takes a few seconds up to $D = `r format(beta_Dmax, big.mark = ",")`$.
  NumPyro on the CPU is faster than tipsae per fit, and per effective draw at all sizes but
  $D = 500$, where the two were about equal. On this machine the
  Apple GPU (Metal) was slower than the CPU at every size measured. No NVIDIA GPU was available,
  so CUDA was not measured.
- At $D \ge 500$, the smallest ESS of both MCMC methods with default settings was only a few
  dozen, so their per-fit times understate the time needed for a reliable fit.

## Memory

The memory of a fit is the peak resident set size (RSS) of the R process **and all its child
processes** (INLA runs as a separate program), sampled every 0.1 s, minus the peak of a process
that loads the same packages and data without fitting. `bench::mark()`'s `mem_alloc` is not used:
it counts only memory allocated by R, so it misses INLA, Stan and JAX.

```{r memory-table}
mm <- function(model, methods) {
  x <- sp[sp$model == model & sp$method %in% methods, ]
  w <- reshape(x[, c("method", "D", "peak_increase_mb")], idvar = "D", timevar = "method", direction = "wide")
  w <- w[order(w$D), ]
  out <- data.frame(D = format(w$D, big.mark = ","))
  for (m in methods) out[[method_labels[[m]]]] <- fmt_mb(w[[paste0("peak_increase_mb.", m)]])
  out
}
knitr::kable(mm("sfh", c("fastsae", "sae", "emdi")), row.names = FALSE, align = "rrrr",
             caption = "Spatial Fay-Herriot: increase of the peak memory")
knitr::kable(mm("beta", c("inla", "jax", "metal", "tipsae")), row.names = FALSE, align = "rrrrr",
             caption = "Spatial Beta: increase of the peak memory")
```

- **Spatial Fay-Herriot:** fastsae needs less memory than `sae` and `emdi` at $D = 500$ and
  1,000; at $D = 100$ the differences are within run-to-run noise, and at the largest $D$ its
  margin over `emdi` is small.
- **Spatial Beta:** no method is best at every size. INLA's memory grows slowly with $D$;
  tipsae needs little memory for small $D$ and the most at $D = `r format(beta_Dmax, big.mark = ",")`$;
  NumPyro's 700-900 MB are mostly the Python interpreter and JAX, which is counted here because a
  user pays for it too.

**Limits of the method.** Peaks shorter than the 0.1 s sampling interval can be missed.
Differences of a few tens of MB vary from run to run. On Apple silicon the GPU uses the same
(unified) memory, which RSS does not fully show, so the Metal figures are lower bounds.

---

## Conclusions

- **Spatial Fay-Herriot.** fastsae is not more accurate than `sae` or `emdi`: it fits the same
  estimator and gives the same numbers. It is **faster** (12 to 35 times here for
  $D \ge 500$), uses **less or about the same memory**, and returned a fit for every data set,
  where `sae` and `emdi` stopped with an error in about 1% of all data sets (up to 4% in the
  hardest scenario). In a few data sets near the boundary of $\rho$ its estimate or its MSE
  differs from that of `sae`, as documented.
- **Spatial Beta.** fastsae with INLA is **about as accurate** as tipsae, better with a strong
  spatial effect and slightly worse with a low Beta precision, and **25 to 75 times faster** here
  ($D = 50$ to 1,000). Its memory is not lower than tipsae's for small $D$. The MCMC engine of fastsae gives
  the same estimates as INLA and is faster than tipsae, but with default settings neither MCMC
  method converged reliably.
- Every conclusion holds for these scenarios, these defaults and this machine. The accuracy study
  uses $D \le 500$ (SFH) and $D = 50$ (Beta), and the parameter values were chosen for this study.

## Reproduce

From the package root, after `R CMD INSTALL . --preclean` (the scripts use the installed fastsae):

```sh
sh benchmarks/eval/run_overnight.sh          # accuracy (6 parallel processes), then speed and memory
WORKERS=4 sh benchmarks/eval/run_overnight.sh 00:00   # same, starting at midnight
```

The scripts are in [`benchmarks/eval/`](https://github.com/ridsonap/fastsae/tree/main/benchmarks/eval):
`eval_common.R` (scenarios, data and fits), `sim_accuracy.R` (one task per scenario, method and block
of replicates, resumable) and `bench_resources.R` (one process per cell). The run behind this page
took about 2.7 hours for the accuracy study and 1.7 hours for speed and memory. Seeds are fixed: the
design of scenario $k$ uses seed $1000 + k$, replicate $r$ seed $10^5 k + r$.

## Machine and versions

```{r meta}
m <- res$meta
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Item = c("Date", "Machine", "RAM", "OS", "R", "Packages", "Python", "Threads", "Settings"),
  Value = c(
    format(m$date), sprintf("%s, %d cores", m$cpu, m$cores), sprintf("%.0f GB", m$ram_gb), m$os, m$r,
    paste(names(m$versions), m$versions, collapse = ", "),
    paste(names(m$python), m$python, collapse = ", "),
    sprintf("OMP_NUM_THREADS %s; INLA single-threaded (hb_area); tipsae chains one after another; NumPyro chains on the CPU", m$omp_threads),
    paste(m$settings, collapse = "; ")
  )
), row.names = FALSE, align = "ll")
```
